title: Bloom Filter
description: Build a Bloom filter that remembers a set in a fixed number of bits, with no false negatives.
statement:
Build `BloomFilter(size, hashes, seed=0)`: a set that answers "have I seen this item?" using a fixed number of bits. It may say yes for an item that was never added (a false positive) but never says no for one that was.

- The filter holds exactly `size` bits and must not keep the items themselves. Items are strings.
- `add(item)` sets `hashes` bits. `might_contain(item)` returns `True` only if all of that item's bits are set, otherwise `False`.
- Derive an item's bit positions with `hashlib.sha256` from the seed and the item, for example from the digest of `f"{seed}:{i}:{item}"` for each `i` in `range(hashes)`, reduced into `range(size)`. Python's built-in `hash()` changes between runs, so do not use it.
- The seed goes into every hash: filters with different seeds make different mistakes.
- With `BloomFilter(10_000, 7)` holding 1000 items, fewer than 30 out of 1000 other items may be reported as present.

**Example**

```python
bf = BloomFilter(10_000, 7)
bf.might_contain("alice")   # False
bf.add("alice")
bf.might_contain("alice")   # True
bf.might_contain("bob")     # False (1 item in 10,000 bits: a false positive is practically impossible)
```
tests:
members = [f"user-{i}" for i in range(1000)]
strangers = [f"visitor-{i}" for i in range(1000)]

tests.name: the example: absent, then added, then present
tests.code:
bf = BloomFilter(10_000, 7)
assert bf.might_contain("alice") is False, "an empty filter must answer False"
bf.add("alice")
assert bf.might_contain("alice") is True, "alice was added, so might_contain must answer True"
assert bf.might_contain("bob") is False, "bob was never added and the filter is nearly empty"

tests.name: an empty filter says False for everything
tests.code:
empty = BloomFilter(10_000, 7)
assert [item for item in members if empty.might_contain(item)] == []

tests.name: no false negatives: 1000 added items are all reported present
tests.code:
bf = BloomFilter(10_000, 7)
for item in members:
    bf.add(item)
assert [item for item in members if not bf.might_contain(item)] == []

tests.name: few false positives: fewer than 30 of 1000 strangers (10,000 bits, 7 hashes, 1000 items)
tests.code:
bf = BloomFilter(10_000, 7)
for item in members:
    bf.add(item)
found = [item for item in strangers if bf.might_contain(item)]
assert len(found) < 30, f"{len(found)} of 1000 items that were never added were reported present; about 8 are expected, so check that the 7 hashes differ and spread over all 10,000 bits"

tests.name: the same seed gives the same answers; a different seed makes different mistakes
tests.code:
def build(seed):
    bf = BloomFilter(2_000, 3, seed=seed)
    for item in members[:300]:
        bf.add(item)
    return bf

probes = [f"probe-{i}" for i in range(600)]
first, again, other = build(1), build(1), build(2)
answers = lambda bf: [bf.might_contain(probe) for probe in probes]
assert answers(first) == answers(again), "two filters with the same settings and items must answer identically"
assert answers(first) != answers(other), "filters with different seeds should be wrong about different items; is the seed part of every hash?"

tests.name: `hashes` is the number of bits per item: a nearly empty 1-hash filter errs far more often than an 8-hash one
the filter has only `size` bits: a full 8-bit filter says True for everything
tests.code:
tiny = BloomFilter(8, 2)
for i in range(100):
    tiny.add(f"x-{i}")
assert all(tiny.might_contain(f"never-added-{i}") for i in range(50)), "100 items in 8 bits must set every bit, so every question gets True (do not store the items)"

tests.name: a one-bit filter works: positions are reduced modulo the size
tests.code:
one = BloomFilter(1, 3)
assert one.might_contain("a") is False
one.add("a")
assert one.might_contain("a") is True
assert one.might_contain("anything else") is True, "with one bit, adding any item sets the only bit"

tests.name: empty strings and non-ASCII text are valid items
tests.code:
bf = BloomFilter(1_000, 5)
odd = ["", "h\u00e9llo", "\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e", "\U0001F642", "a b\tc\n"]
for item in odd:
    bf.add(item)
assert [item for item in odd if not bf.might_contain(item)] == []

hints: You cannot store the items. What could you store instead, so that one item leaves several traces, and a missing trace proves the item was never added?

Keep `size` bits. For an item, compute `hashes` positions in `range(size)`: hash `f"{seed}:{i}:{item}"` with SHA-256 for each `i`, turn the digest into an integer and take it modulo `size`. `add` sets those bits; `might_contain` checks that all of them are set.

Do not use the built-in `hash()` (it changes between runs). Make every one of the `hashes` positions depend on `i`; if they were all equal you would have one hash function and many more false positives.
explanation:
**The idea.** A Bloom filter is an array of `size` bits. To add an item, compute `hashes` positions from it and set those bits. To ask about an item, compute the same positions: if any bit is 0 the item was certainly never added (so there are no false negatives); if all are 1 it was probably added, but other items may have set those bits by chance (a false positive).

**Deriving k hash functions.** One SHA-256 call per position, with the loop counter `i` in the input, gives `hashes` independent-looking positions; the seed gives whole families of them. Python's built-in `hash()` of a string is randomised per process, so a filter saved by one process could not be read by another. Reduce with `% size` so every position fits.

**Sizing.** With `m` bits, `k` hashes and `n` items the false-positive rate is about `(1 - e^(-kn/m))^k`. For 10,000 bits, 7 hashes and 1000 items that is about 0.8%, which is why the test allows 3%. For a given `m` and `n`, the best `k` is about `(m / n) * ln 2`.

**Limits.** You cannot remove an item (clearing a bit could erase another item's trace); a counting Bloom filter keeps small counters instead of bits. Real uses: skipping disk reads for keys that certainly do not exist (LSM-tree databases), a crawler's "seen this URL?" check, cheap cache-miss tests. Follow-up: how would two nodes combine their filters? (Bitwise OR of two filters with the same size, hashes and seed.)
